analysis.one_liner: Grants the Keystone XL pipeline standing legal authorization to cross the border without a presidential permit.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 1 sponsor and 147 Republican cosponsors but never received a hearing or a vote, dying when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: After the president revoked Keystone XL's cross-border permit, this bill would have written the authorization directly into law: TransCanada Keystone Pipeline could build, connect, operate, and maintain the pipeline's border crossing in Phillips County, Montana, and no presidential permit would ever be required for it. The bill went to three House committees and was sent to three subcommittees, and that is where it stayed. It never got a hearing or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the biggest beneficiary would be TransCanada (now TC Energy), the pipeline developer, which would have held a permanent legal authorization that no future administration could revoke. Canadian oil sands producers would have gained a dedicated route to move heavy crude to Gulf Coast refineries, Gulf Coast refiners would have gained a cheaper heavy crude supply, and the construction trades would have gained pipeline-building work.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The pipeline developer and oil sands producers

how_it_helps.text: The bill authorizes TransCanada Keystone Pipeline, L.P. to construct, connect, operate, and maintain the pipeline facilities at the U.S.–Canada border in Phillips County, Montana, for importing oil from Canada.

It goes further than a normal permit by stating that no presidential permit under any executive order shall be required for the pipeline's construction, connection, operation, or maintenance — meaning the authorization could not be pulled by a future administration the way the 2019 permit was.

The bill's title — Keystone XL Pipeline Construction and Jobs Preservation Act — frames the pipeline as a jobs measure, and pipeline construction would have generated construction work in Montana, South Dakota, Nebraska, and Texas.

analysis.who_pays: The cost of the pipeline itself would fall on the company, but the public costs would include the spill risk along the pipeline route (including the Ogallala aquifer in Nebraska) and the additional greenhouse gas emissions tied to burning Canadian oil sands crude, which is more carbon-intensive to produce than conventional oil. Taxpayers and landowners along the route would also have absorbed the risks of a project placed beyond ordinary presidential permitting review.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities along the route and the climate

drawbacks.text: The bill would strip executive branch review of a cross-border project: by declaring that no presidential permit is required, it would have removed the single mechanism by which a president can vet and condition an international pipeline crossing.

Keystone XL would carry Canadian oil sands crude, which produces more greenhouse gas emissions over its lifecycle than conventional crude — the central reason climate and environmental groups opposed the project for a decade.

The jobs at stake were mostly temporary construction jobs lasting a year or two of building, with only a small permanent operating crew afterward — which is why the 'jobs preservation' framing drew skepticism even from supporters of pipeline work generally.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main work is not a general energy policy but a single-company authorization: it would convert a revocable presidential permit into a permanent statutory right for one pipeline, insulated from any future administration. The public upside was temporary construction employment and a marginally more secure crude supply; the public costs were permanent — decades of spill risk along the route and additional carbon emissions. Weighing those honestly, the bill transfers a long-term public risk into a durable private asset, and the same project was canceled by its own developer months into this Congress anyway.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees and was parceled out to three subcommittees, never got a hearing or a floor vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended — while the pipeline's developer had already canceled the project in June 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Kelly Armstrong introduced the bill on February 2, 2021, days after the new administration revoked Keystone XL's presidential permit.

It was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, and Natural Resources Committees, and within days was assigned to three subcommittees: Energy, Railroads/Pipelines/Hazardous Materials, and Energy and Mineral Resources.
One sponsor and 147 cosponsors — every one of them a Republican — signed on.
No further action of any kind was taken for the rest of the Congress; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and it expired on January 3, 2023.

The bill was largely overtaken by events: the project's developer, TC Energy, canceled Keystone XL in June 2021 after the permit revocation and years of permitting and court battles, so even a successful bill would have had nothing left to authorize.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything from this bill, because it became law of nothing and the pipeline was dead regardless — its developer canceled it while the bill sat in committee. The parties better off under the actual outcome are the communities, tribes, and landowners along the route who had opposed the pipeline for a decade, and the executive branch's authority to vet border-crossing energy projects, which the bill would have erased.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pipeline opponents; the bill itself changed nothing

for.name: Rep. Kelly Armstrong
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to statutorily authorize Keystone XL after the presidential permit was revoked.

for.name: Kevin McCarthy
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor who helped assemble the bill's introduction with a large bloc of House Republicans.

for.name: 147 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it an entirely Republican-supported measure.

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House floor calendar; the bill never received a hearing or a vote during her speakership.

against.name: Joe Biden
against.what_they_did: Revoked Keystone XL's presidential permit on his first day in office, prompting this bill as a response; never supported the pipeline's construction.

against.name: TC Energy
against.what_they_did: Canceled the Keystone XL project in June 2021, making the bill moot even if it had advanced.

sides.party_line_note: All 148 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; the Democratic majority that controlled the House took no action on the bill at any point in two years.

industries.note: The bill would hand one company a permanent statutory authorization for its border crossing, immune from presidential revocation — converting a revocable government permit into a durable private right. The public's corresponding cost is long-term spill and climate risk with only temporary construction jobs in return.

A built Keystone XL would have given producers a dedicated, lower-cost route to move heavy crude to Gulf Coast markets. The public tradeoff is that oil sands crude is more carbon-intensive than conventional oil.
Refiners configured to process heavy Canadian crude would have gained a cheaper, more secure feedstock — a cost saving that could partially pass through to consumers.
Construction unions supported the project for the welding and pipeline-building work it would have created, though most of those jobs were temporary.

industries.industry: Landowners, tribes, and communities along the route
industries.note: The bill would override the permitting review these groups had used for a decade to contest the route, leaving them with the spill risk and eminent domain fights and none of the review.
